newsitem.title: CHINA: China dissident freed after 2-1/2 yrs labour.
newsitem.headline: China dissident freed after 2-1/2 yrs labour.

text.p: China on Thursday freed dissident Tong Yi, former secretary to jailed veteran democracy activist Wei Jingsheng, after she completed a 2-1/2 year term of "re-education through labour".
"My term of labour was very harsh," Tong said in a telephone interview from her home in the central Chinese city of Wuhan.
Tong had been ordered to serve the administrative punishment of re-education through labour in Wuhan following charges of forging a seal and for being an "accessory" to her mentor, Wei.

Tong, a student activist during the ill-fated pro-democracy demonstrations of 1989, said she had no firm plans following her release, but was eager to catch up with events in China and abroad after more than two years with scant access to news.
"They only said one thing to me when I was released today and that was 'Don't try to set yourself against the government'," she said. "I don't know what that means."
The authorities had set no formal restrictions such as limiting her freedom to travel in China, she said.
"I can't rule out the possibility of going to Beijing," she said.

Tong was detained in Beijing on April 4, 1994, four days after police detained Wei. She had worked for Wei as his secretary and translator after he was released on parole in September, 1993, six months before the end of a 15-year term for "counter-revolution" or subversion.
Wei, regarded as the father of China's struggling democracy movement, was sentenced to 14 years in prison last December on new charges of counter-revolutionary crimes.
Tong said she had been held for nine months in a Beijing detention centre before being ordered to serve 2-1/2 years of re-education through labour in a her home town of Wuhan.

Re-education through labour is an administrative punishment recently favoured by Chinese authorities as a means of dealing with dissidents since it avoids the need for a formal trial under Chinese law.
Her labour included folding cardboard boxes, sewing and textile finishing, she said.
"Every day was very boring," she said.
She said she had been denied access to newspapers until early this year, and was among the last to learn of Wei's new sentence.
"I am very concerned about him, and I will continue to be very concerned," she said. "Wei Jingsheng is a very determined person and I am confident he will face this new challenge."

The Hong Kong-based Information Centre of Human Rights and Democratic Movement in China said one of Wei's sisters had visited him on September 19 in jail near Tangshan in northern Hebei province and reported his health was deteriorating.
Wei was suffering from heart problems on an almost daily basis as well as from persistent high blood pressure, it quoted Wei's sister as saying.
In addition, inmates in neighbouring cells appeared to be deliberately making a noise to prevent him from sleeping, thus further exacerbating his poor health, she said.
Wei was first jailed in 1979 for 15 years for his role in Beijing's 1978-79 Democracy Wall movement, when he described senior leader Deng Xiaoping as a dictator.
During his six months of freedom, Wei often and openly criticised the government and said he had no regrets about taking a public stand.
